title: Free emotional intelligence test (EQ test) with scores for 4 skills — cv.cm
description: Free EQ test online. Rate 20 statements to score your self-awareness, self-management, empathy and relationship skills, with what each score means and how to build it. No sign-up.
lede: Emotional intelligence is the skill of noticing, understanding and handling emotions, your own and other people's. Rate 20 statements and see your score in each of its four areas.
about: This test follows the four areas of Daniel Goleman's model of emotional intelligence: self-awareness (knowing what you feel and why), self-management (handling those feelings), social awareness (reading other people) and relationship management (getting along, influencing and resolving conflict).

The statements were written for cv.cm. It is a self-report check, not the licensed EQ-i or MSCEIT, and a self-report shows how you see yourself. Each area is scored from 0 to 100: below 40 is low, above 60 high. Unlike IQ, these are skills, and they improve with practice.

faq.q: What is a good EQ score?
faq.a: There is no pass mark here. A score above 60 in an area means you see that skill as a strength; below 40 marks the area most worth practising. Look at the balance between the four areas rather than one number.
Yes. Naming your feelings, pausing before you react, asking people how they see a situation and listening without planning your answer are skills that grow with practice.

faq.q: Is EQ more important than IQ?
faq.a: They measure different things. IQ tests reasoning; EQ is about handling emotions and people. Both matter, and EQ matters most in work that depends on teamwork, leadership and service.

faq.q: How accurate is a self-report EQ test?
faq.a: It shows how you see yourself, which can differ from how others see you. For a fuller picture, ask a few people who know you well to answer the questions about you.

items: I can usually name exactly what I'm feeling, not just "good" or "bad".
When I'm upset, I can calm myself down before I say something I regret.
I often notice how someone feels before they say anything.
I can tell someone they're wrong without damaging our relationship.
My mood often changes and I can't tell why.
When something annoys me, it tends to ruin the rest of my day.
I find it hard to see a situation from someone else's side when I disagree.
Conflicts with people tend to get worse once I'm involved.
I know which situations tend to make me anxious or angry.
I can stay calm and think clearly under pressure.
People often tell me I'm a good listener.
I find it easy to make people feel comfortable around me.
I'm often surprised by how strongly I react to things.
I act on impulse and then wish I had waited.
I miss it when friends are going through a hard time until they tell me.
I avoid difficult conversations even when they need to happen.
I understand how my feelings affect the way I work and treat others.
After a setback, I can pick myself up and keep going.
I can tell when someone says they're fine but isn't.
When two people disagree, I can help them find common ground.

self.low: Your feelings often take you by surprise. Try naming your emotion a few times a day, as precisely as you can ("irritated", "disappointed", "nervous"), and noticing what set it off.
self.mid: You usually know what you feel, though strong or mixed emotions can still catch you out. Keep checking in with yourself in busy or tense moments.
self.high: You know your emotions well, what triggers them and how they shape what you do. That self-knowledge is the base for every other emotional skill.

regulate.low: Strong feelings tend to drive what you do. A pause of a few slow breaths, or a rule to sleep on angry replies, gives you room to choose your response.
regulate.mid: You keep your cool most of the time, but stress or tiredness can tip you over. Notice your early warning signs and act on them sooner.
regulate.high: You stay steady under pressure, recover from setbacks and rarely act on impulse. People can rely on you when things get tense.

empathy.low: Other people's feelings can be hard for you to read. Ask more questions ("How are you finding this?") and watch faces and tone, not just words.
empathy.mid: You pick up on how people feel when you pay attention, but you can miss quieter signals when you're busy or disagree.
empathy.high: You read people well and understand their point of view, even when you disagree. People feel heard around you.

social.low: Handling conflict and difficult conversations is a growth area for you. Start small: give honest, kind feedback about one thing, and say what you need clearly.
social.mid: You get along well with most people. Practising the harder parts, like conflict, feedback and bringing people together, will make you even stronger.
social.high: You build trust, handle conflict calmly and help people work together. Teams and friends often count on you to keep things running smoothly.
